questions.q: Which statement describes what happens to an element when it is oxidised?

options.A: It loses electrons and its oxidation number increases.
options.B: It gains electrons and its oxidation number increases.
options.C: It loses electrons and its oxidation number decreases.
options.D: It gains electrons and its oxidation number decreases.

questions.solution: Oxidation is loss of electrons. Losing negative electrons makes the element more positive, so its oxidation number rises. (Mixing up the two definitions is the usual slip: gain of electrons and a fall in oxidation number is reduction.)

questions.q: Which statement about an oxidising agent is correct?

options.A: It donates electrons and is itself oxidised.
options.B: It accepts electrons and is itself oxidised.
options.C: It accepts electrons and is itself reduced.
options.D: It donates electrons and is itself reduced.

questions.solution: An oxidising agent oxidises something else by taking electrons from it. Gaining those electrons means the oxidising agent itself is reduced. (A common slip is to think an oxidising agent is oxidised.)

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in oxygen difluoride, \(\mathrm{OF_{2}}\)?
questions.solution: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so it is always −1. Two fluorines give −2, and the compound is neutral, so oxygen must be +2. (Assuming oxygen is always −2 is the usual slip; this is one of its exceptions.)

questions.q: In which species does chlorine have the highest oxidation number?
questions.solution: In \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}O_{7}}\): \(2x = +14\), so +7. In \(\mathrm{ClO_{2}}\): +4. In \(\mathrm{HClO}\): +1. In \(\mathrm{ClO_{3}^{-}}\): \(x - 6 = -1\), so +5. The highest is +7, in \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}O_{7}}\). (Forgetting to share the oxygen total between the two chlorine atoms leads to +14, which is impossible.)

questions.q: Which species is the reducing agent in this reaction? \(\mathrm{SO_{2} + Br_{2} + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}SO_{4} + 2HBr}\)
questions.solution: Sulfur goes from +4 in \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) to +6 in \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\): it is oxidised, so \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) gives electrons to bromine and is the reducing agent. Bromine goes from 0 to −1: it is reduced, so \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) is the oxidising agent. (Picking the species that is reduced is the common slip.)

In a disproportionation the same element in one species is both oxidised and reduced. Chlorine in \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) (0) goes to −1 in \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) and to +5 in \(\mathrm{ClO_{3}^{-}}\). The displacement and the iron(III)/iodide reactions are redox between two different elements; silver chloride precipitation is not redox at all. (Choosing a displacement because chlorine is both a reactant and a product is the common slip.)

questions.q: Which reaction is not a redox reaction?
questions.solution: Chromium is +6 in \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}}\) and still +6 in \(\mathrm{CrO_{4}^{2-}}\); no element changes oxidation number, so this is an acid–base change, not redox. Each of the others has a change: Zn 0 to +2, O −1 to −2 and 0, Mg 0 to +2. (The colour change from orange to yellow tempts students to call it redox.)

questions.q: Which is the correct half-equation for the reduction of nitrate ions to nitrogen monoxide, \(\mathrm{NO}\), in acidic solution?
questions.solution: Nitrogen goes from +5 to +2, so 3 electrons are gained, on the left. Two \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) balance the oxygen and 4 \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) the hydrogen. Charge check: \(-1 + 4 - 3 = 0\) on each side. (Putting the electrons on the right is the common slip: that would be an oxidation, and the charges do not balance.)

questions.q: Acidified manganate(VII) ions oxidise sulfur dioxide to sulfate ions and are reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\). Which is the balanced overall equation?
questions.solution: Half-equations: \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-} + 8H^{+} + 5e^{-} \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_{2}O}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_{2} + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow SO_{4}^{2-} + 4H^{+} + 2e^{-}}\). Multiply by 2 and 5 to transfer 10 electrons, add, then cancel 16 \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) against 20 and 8 \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) against 10. That leaves 2 \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) on the left and 4 \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) on the right. (Adding without cancelling the water and hydrogen ions is the common slip.)

questions.q: Iodate(V) ions, \(\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}\), are reduced to iodine, \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\), in acidic solution. How many electrons does each \(\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}\) ion gain?
questions.solution: Iodine goes from +5 in \(\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}\) to 0 in \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\), so each iodate ion gains 5 electrons. The half-equation is \(\mathrm{2IO_{3}^{-} + 12H^{+} + 10e^{-} \rightarrow I_{2} + 6H_{2}O}\), which has two iodate ions. (A common slip is to give the electrons for the whole half-equation, 10.)

questions.q: What is the formula of sodium chlorate(I)?
questions.solution: The (I) gives chlorine an oxidation number of +1. With sodium +1 and one oxygen −2, \(\mathrm{NaClO}\) is neutral: \(+1 + 1 - 2 = 0\). (\(\mathrm{NaClO_{3}}\) is sodium chlorate(V); reading the numeral as the number of oxygen atoms is a common slip.)

questions.q: In which change is the transition metal reduced?
questions.solution: Manganese goes from +7 in \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) to +6 in \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{2-}}\): a fall, so it is reduced (it gains one electron). Vanadium goes +4 to +5 and chromium +3 to +6 (both oxidised); in dichromate to chromate chromium stays at +6. (Judging by the ion charge, which becomes more negative in several of these, is the common slip.)

questions.q: \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of an iron(II) solution reacts with \(22.50\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.0200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) acidified potassium manganate(VII). \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-} + 8H^{+} + 5Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_{2}O + 5Fe^{3+}}\). What is the concentration of iron(II) ions?
questions.solution: Moles of \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) \(= 0.0200 \times 0.02250 = 4.50 \times 10^{-4}\). Each reacts with 5 \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), so moles of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) \(= 2.25 \times 10^{-3}\). Concentration \(= 2.25 \times 10^{-3} \div 0.0250 = 0.0900\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). (Using a 1 : 1 ratio leads to 0.0180.)

questions.q: A \(0.500\ \text{g}\) sample of brass is dissolved in acid. Excess potassium iodide is added: \(\mathrm{2Cu^{2+} + 4I^{-} \rightarrow 2CuI + I_{2}}\). The iodine released reacts with \(23.60\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sodium thiosulfate: \(\mathrm{I_{2} + 2S_{2}O_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow 2I^{-} + S_{4}O_{6}^{2-}}\). What is the percentage by mass of copper in the brass? (\(A_{\text{r}}\) Cu = 63.5)
questions.solution: Moles of thiosulfate \(= 0.100 \times 0.02360 = 2.36 \times 10^{-3}\). From the equations, 2 \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) give 1 \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\), which reacts with 2 \(\mathrm{S_{2}O_{3}^{2-}}\): copper and thiosulfate are 1 : 1. Mass of Cu \(= 2.36 \times 10^{-3} \times 63.5 = 0.1499\ \text{g}\), so the percentage \(= 0.1499 \div 0.500 \times 100 = 30.0\%\). (Taking Cu : thiosulfate as 1 : 2 leads to 15.0%.)

questions.q: In an iodine–thiosulfate titration, why is starch indicator added only when the solution has become pale yellow, near the end point?

options.A: With a lot of iodine present, starch forms a complex that releases the iodine only slowly, which makes the end point hard to judge.
options.B: Starch is oxidised by a high concentration of iodine.
options.C: Starch reacts with thiosulfate ions, so adding it early would use up thiosulfate.
options.D: The blue-black colour only forms once all the thiosulfate has reacted.

questions.solution: Starch added while much iodine remains forms an intense blue-black complex that gives the iodine back to the thiosulfate only slowly, so the colour lingers and the end point is blurred. Added near the end, it gives a sharp change from blue-black to colourless. (Thinking starch reacts with one of the reagents is the common slip: it is only an indicator.)

questions.q: Why is an iron(II) solution acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, rather than hydrochloric acid, before titration with potassium manganate(VII)?

options.A: Manganate(VII) would oxidise chloride ions to chlorine, so less manganate(VII) would be used and the result would be too low.
options.B: Manganate(VII) would oxidise chloride ions to chlorine, so more manganate(VII) would be used and the result would be too high.
options.C: Hydrochloric acid is too weak to provide the hydrogen ions needed.
options.D: Chloride ions would reduce iron(III) back to iron(II), so the colour change would not be seen.

questions.solution: Manganate(VII) (\(E^{\ominus} = +1.51\ \text{V}\)) can oxidise \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) (\(+1.36\ \text{V}\)). Some manganate(VII) would then be used on chloride as well as on iron(II), so the titre, and the calculated iron(II), would be too high. (Getting the direction of the error wrong is the common slip.)

questions.q: Why is no separate indicator needed when iron(II) ions are titrated with acidified potassium manganate(VII)?

options.A: The iron(III) ions formed are deep red, so the solution changes colour at the end point.
options.B: The reaction is too fast for an indicator to respond.
options.C: Manganate(VII) is purple and is reduced to almost colourless manganese(II), so the first permanent pink colour shows the end point.
options.D: Manganate(VII) would oxidise any indicator added before reacting with iron(II).

questions.solution: Each drop of purple \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) is decolourised while iron(II) remains. Once it has all reacted, the next drop of excess manganate(VII) gives a permanent pale pink: the titration indicates its own end point. (Iron(III) ions in this dilute solution are only very pale yellow, so they cannot show the end point.)
